subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: It was one in the morning and my app kept crashing, but only sometimes. Pranav, you had gone to bed, so here is what I did, now that I have finally slept. First I made it crash on purpose, until I saw it happened only when the name field was empty. That was my repeatable case. Second, I cut everything except that one screen. It still crashed. Third, I changed one thing: I gave the field a default. No crash. I wrote each step in my notes: "empty name, crash; default set, fine." Without that list I would have gone in circles, tired as I was. In the morning I read my own list and fixed the check properly. Sunaina

qa.q: When did the app crash?
qa.a: The app crashed only when the name field was empty.

qa.q: How does Sunaina feel about writing each step in the notes?
qa.a: Sunaina feels relieved and grateful to the list, because being tired at one in the morning would have meant going in circles without it.

qa.q: What made the problem easier for Sunaina to solve?
qa.a: Making the crash repeatable, cutting the app down to one screen and changing one thing at a time while writing each result in notes.

qa.q: What might Pranav think of the story if Pranav had been awake and offering many suggestions?
qa.a: Pranav might have offered several guesses at once, which would have made it harder to tell which change made the difference.

grounding: Shows a problem solver making a fault repeatable, isolating it, changing one thing at a time and noting each result.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: At two in the morning the light was still on under Uma's door in the hostel. The study group's marks sheet showed a total that was forty out. I, Lakshmi, sat on the spare chair with my tea and watched. Uma did not shout at the screen. She copied the sheet, made the wrong total appear again in the copy, then deleted columns until the total came right: column D. Then she changed one cell at a time and wrote each result on a scrap of paper: "D7 is text, not a number." I could not tell if she was pleased or too tired to care. She fixed D7, the total matched, and she stuck the scrap above her desk.

qa.q: What was wrong with the study group's marks sheet?
qa.a: The sheet showed a total that was forty out.

qa.q: How can you tell that Uma is patient, and what is uncertain about her mood?
qa.a: She works step by step without shouting, but the narrator could not tell if she was pleased or too tired to care.

qa.q: What would you advise Uma to do if the fault comes back on another sheet?
qa.a: She can follow the same list on a copy: make the wrong total appear again, narrow it down, change one cell at a time and note each result.

qa.q: What is it like for Lakshmi watching Uma work at two in the morning?
qa.a: Lakshmi sits quietly with tea and is curious, but cannot tell what Uma feels inside, only what her careful steps show.

grounding: Shows a problem solver reproducing a fault on a copy, isolating a column, changing one cell at a time and writing down each result.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Tuesday night. Mohit, twenty, had a college robotics demo on Friday, and his robot arm jerked randomly. He'd spent two hours changing things and was going in circles, exhausted and alone in the lab.
Wednesday. His senior, Baljeet, sat with him. "First, can you make it jerk on purpose?" After twenty tries, Mohit found it happened only when the arm turned left fast. "Now narrow it down: motor, wire or code?" They swapped the motor. Still jerked. Then Mohit wrote each test in a notebook.
Thursday. He changed only the code's speed limit for left turns and tested. Smooth. He tested again ten times, noting each one. By evening, the notebook showed exactly what had fixed it.

qa.q: When did the robot arm jerk?
qa.a: Only when the arm turned left fast.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel on Tuesday night?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and alone, going in circles after two hours of changing things.

qa.q: Which steps helped Mohit solve it?
qa.a: Making the fault repeatable, narrowing it down between motor, wire and code, changing one thing at a time and writing each test in a notebook.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Mohit's notebook by Thursday?
qa.a: Baljeet would likely feel pleased, seeing a clear record of the steps that found the fault.

grounding: Shows over days a student making a fault repeatable, narrowing it down, changing one thing at a time and noting each result.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: Mridul, you're struggling with your final-year project, so let me tell you about your cousin Jomon. I was his uncle, and I let him use my workshop when he was twenty, studying electrical engineering. His radio project kept buzzing. For three nights he changed everything at once, and by the third he was near tears, tired and fed up. I made him tea and said, "Can you make it buzz whenever you want?" He could: only when the volume was high. "Good. Now find where." He tested each section, one at a time, and wrote results on the wall with chalk. By midnight the chalk showed it: a loose earth wire. One change. No more buzz. He left the chalk marks there for years.

qa.q: What did Jomon find was causing the buzz?
qa.a: A loose earth wire.

qa.q: How was Jomon feeling on the third night?
qa.a: He was near tears, tired and fed up after changing everything at once.

qa.q: Which choice in the story led to the fix?
qa.a: Making the buzz happen on purpose, testing one section at a time and writing results in chalk on the wall.

qa.q: How might the uncle have seen Jomon's first three nights?
qa.a: The uncle saw circular guessing driven by tiredness, and offered tea and a simple question instead of criticism.

grounding: An elder recalls a young engineer who stopped guessing, made the fault repeatable, isolated it and changed one thing.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: Hansa, twenty-one, was the only one on duty at the college's computer lab on the night before exams, and the printer kept jamming. Thirty students were waiting in line to print their project reports, and the technician, Varun, was at home with fever and could only help by phone. Her first instinct was to open everything and pull at paper. Instead she took a breath. She printed one page. Jam. She printed from a different computer. Jam. So it wasn't the computer. She switched to thinner paper. No jam. She wrote each test on the back of a sheet. When Varun called, she read him her notes. "It's the paper tray," he said. "Well done." The line started moving.

qa.q: How many students were waiting to print?
qa.a: Thirty students were waiting in line.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when the printer first jammed?
qa.a: She felt pressured and tempted to panic, with an instinct to pull everything apart.

qa.q: How did Hansa narrow the problem down?
qa.a: She repeated the jam, ruled out the computer, changed only the paper and wrote each test down.

qa.q: How might Varun feel on the phone, hearing Hansa's notes?
qa.a: Varun would likely feel relieved and impressed, since clear notes let him identify the paper tray from home.

grounding: Shows a student under pressure making a fault repeatable, isolating it one change at a time and noting results.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: At eleven at night in the Behala flat, Binita's sewing machine started skipping stitches, and Vandana's blouse had to be ready by morning for a cousin's haldi. Vandana had fallen asleep on the divan. Tired and alone with the whirr, Binita wanted to fiddle with everything at once. Instead she tore a strip of scrap cotton and sewed a test line. Every fifth or sixth stitch skipped. Good: she could make it happen on demand. On the back of an old electricity bill she wrote: 1. New needle. Sewed a strip. Still skipping. 2. Rethreaded the top. Still skipping. 3. Took out the bobbin case: a ball of lint inside. Cleaned it, sewed a strip. Clean line, fifty stitches, no gaps. She circled number 3, yawned, and went back to the blouse. At 1:20 she laid it, finished, beside Vandana's phone.

qa.q: What did Binita find inside the bobbin case?
qa.a: A ball of lint.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the machine started skipping at eleven?
qa.a: Binita was tired and a bit lonely with Vandana asleep, and tempted to fiddle with everything at once in a rush.

qa.q: Why did writing each step on the bill help?
qa.a: Each change was tested alone and noted, so Binita didn't go round in circles while tired and knew exactly that the lint was the fault.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel waking up to the blouse beside the phone?
qa.a: Vandana would likely be relieved and grateful, perhaps without knowing how late Binita worked to fix the machine.

grounding: Illustrates making a fault repeat on demand, changing one thing at a time and writing down each result, which prevents circular guessing when tired.
